sessions.title: Congestion Control for Cellular Wireless Networks
sessions.listing_title: Congestion Control for Cellular Wireless Networks
sessions.description:
Cellular networks exhibit significant variations in
bottleneck link rates even over short time durations.
One would therefore expect that an active queue
management (AQM) scheme running at the cellular
bottleneck router, sending explicit congestion
notification (ECN) signals to senders using direct
knowledge of the time-varying link capacity, would
achieve higher throughput and lower delays than
end-to-end approaches. Yet, recent work has shown that
schemes like Cubic-over-sfqCoDel do not significantly
outperform end-to-end methods like Sprout and Verus.

We hypothesize that a well-designed signaling scheme
running at the cellular bottleneck link, working in
concert with a suitable endpoint algorithm, can
out-perform prior end-to-end and network-assisted
(AQM) strategies. Our hypothesis is based on two key
insights. First, unlike end-to-end approaches, a
router-based scheme can directly estimate link
capacity, without relying on end-to-end bandwidth
measurements which fundamentally require some queue
buildup; on cellular networks, this queue buildup can
add significant delays when link capacity abruptly
decreases. Second, existing ECN-based AQM schemes send
indications only when the sender should reduce its
rate, but not when an increase is possible. The
problem in cellular networks is that the rate can
increase quickly, faster than endpoints (particularly
with linear or even Cubic-like increase) can discover
solely via end-to-end methods.

This BOF is an opportunity to discuss these issues.
The BOF will help formalize the constraints of the
problem and formulate ways in which the community
should evaluate congestion control protocols in
cellular networks. To kick things off in this BoF and
frame future discussions, we will use as motivation a
recently published HotNets position paper on
Accel-Brake Control (ABC) [1].

ABC integrates a simple and deployable signaling
scheme at cellular base stations with an endpoint
mechanism to respond to these signals. The idea is for
the base station to enable each sender to achieve a
computed target rate by marking each packet with an
“accelerate" or “brake" notification,
which causes the sender to either slightly increase or
slightly reduce its congestion window. ABC is designed
to rapidly acquire any capacity that opens up, a
common occurrence in cellular networks, while
responding promptly to congestion.

It is challenging to properly evaluate congestion
control over cellular network paths, especially if it
involves in-network mechanisms, because it is not easy
to deploy even a test network running new
network-layer mechanisms. Simulation is one approach,
but it is not clear how representative results from
cellular simulations are. Another possibility is to
use trace-based emulation, where the traces are
gathered from real-world cellular networks and
replayed via a network emulator on top of which real
implementations of endpoints and Linux router software
run. This BOF will discuss the collection and use of
traces to further research and development in this
area using a tool like Mahimahi [2].

[1] Prateesh Goyal, Mohammad Alizadeh, Hari
Balakrishnan, "Rethinking Congestion Control for
Cellular Networks,” 16th ACM Workshop on Hot
Topics in Networks (HotNets), Palo Alto, CA, November
2017. http://nms.csail.mit.edu/papers/index.php?detail=248

[2] Mahimahi — http://mahimahi.mit.edu/

sessions.title: Kernel TLS handshakes for HTTPS DDoS mitigation
sessions.listing_title: Kernel TLS handshakes for HTTPS DDoS mitigation
sessions.description:
Efforts to offload TLS have resulted in KTLS [0]. KTLS focuses mostly on zero-copy data transfers and only offloads encryption and decryption and ignores TLS handshakes.


However, TLS handshakes are susceptible to DDos attacks which are very effective at depleting resources. To alleviate this we ported onto the Tempesta FW a user-space TLS library to the kernel [1]. The TLS library porting took only 1 human month showing that it is quite easy to move TLS code into the kernel.


In our work we overcame memory allocation issues and other performance issues. We optimized the TLS code and merged the TLS handshakes code of the ported library with Linux kTLS. In this talk we'll discuss the performance issues which we had to solve, the resulting performance improvements for TLS handshakes which we got in Tempesta FW in comparison, and compare the results with TLS handshakes with traditional HTTP accelerators. Further directions in optimization of TLS handshakes on commodity hardware also will be covered.


[0]. Kernel TLS (Transport Layer Security) Socket, Netdev 1.2,
http://www.netdevconf.info/1.2/session.html?dave-watson


[1]. Kernel HTTP/TCP/IP stack for HTTP DDoS mitigation, Netdev 2.1,
https://www.netdevconf.info/2.1/session.html?krizhanovsky

sessions.title: Subscriber Billing System Over Commodity Hardware
sessions.listing_title: Subscriber Billing System Over Commodity Hardware
sessions.description:
At Verizon we have built powerful billing system using
the Linux TC architecture. Typically such systems are
constructed with very expensive proprietary hardware
and software both of which are inflexible. With the
proprietary systems, new user service plan creation
process is constrained by what the vendor provides and
at times requires overhaul of both the proprietary
hardware and software. Utilizing commodity X86 based
hardware, the Linux kernel TC subsystem and user
control we were able to achieve our goals; we are able
to quickly invent new service plans and build
comprehensive billing enforcements around them. In
this paper we will provide a high level discussion of
our architecture, the challenges we faced in building
the system and changes we made to the Linux kernel and
user APIs to achieve our goals. All our patches are
already upstream.

sessions.title: Communication Groups in TIPC
sessions.listing_title: Communication Groups in TIPC
sessions.description:
TIPC provides a very performant and scalable multicast
service, which however has been missing
socket-to-socket flow control. This had the effect
that messages might be dropped at the receiving end
because of socket buffer overflow.

In our effort to overcome this problem, we realized
that the introduced sliding window based flow control
could be used even for other types of message
transport provided by TIPC: datagram unicast and
anycast. This lead us to redefine what was initially a
multicast group to what we now call a "Communication
Group", where all sorts of reliable messaging is
possible. We also realized that it would be possible
to leverage the TIPC service tracking feature to let
group members subscribe for join/leave events from
other members.

The final result was a simple, but powerful, kernel
based brokerless message bus. We think this feature
could be useful both as is and as a base for other
message buses wanting to provide a brokerless service.
The feature is present in Linux 4.14 and onwards.

sessions.title: BBRx: Extending BBR for Customized TCP Performance
sessions.listing_title: BBRx: Extending BBR for Customized TCP Performance
sessions.description:
The most dominant Internet Protocol, TCP, has its
performance tied to the attributes of the network it
deployed on; in the past decades many congestion
detection and estimation techniques have been proposed
to improve TCP performance over various network links.
These techniques have depended on packet loss or delay
sensing to autonomously balance between fairness and
peak performance. More recent congestion
detection/estimation approaches incorporate online
and/or offline learning of the congestion states to
achieve their end goals. This talk introduces a
practical way to apply online-learning on TCP
congestion control domain without tightly coupling
them together.


In late 2016, Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip time
(BBR) congestion control has been presented as an
improvement, with the promise of higher throughputs
and lower delays as compared to other TCP congestion
control algorithms. We extend BBR, referred to as BBRx
in this paper, to react to the path RTT in addition to
the bottleneck bandwidth to help finding an optimal
throughput-delay operation point in wireless
environment.

In order to ensure BBRx is continuously operating in
an optimal point in ever changing network conditions,
TCP flow statistics are monitored in real-time through
Netlink socket by a user-space application which tunes
BBRx parameters with online learning algorithms. The
loosely coupled TCP tuning feedback control loop
provides a novel way to monitor and adjust TCP
parameters per the performance goal in real time while
minimizing the risk of deploying pre-tuned learning
algorithm in the fast path.

Performance of the auto-tuned BBRx is evaluated in LTE
mobile environment as well as wireline environments
compared with CUBIC and BBR. The preliminary results
show the following: BBRx effectively manages the
bottleneck queue yielding a low packet loss rate,
especially when multiple BBRx flows are contending at
a shallow buffer over a bottleneck link; the
auto-tuned BBRx finds an optimal throughput-delay
operation point in LTE environment to maximize
per-flow throughput within a bounded loss rate and
delay.

sessions.title: Using eBPF for RDS filtering
sessions.listing_title: Using eBPF for RDS filtering
sessions.description:
Reliable Datagram Socket (RDS) is an IPC protocol
heavily used in Oracle Clustering and Relational
Database Management Service Applications. There is a
feature request to implement RDS filtering and
firewall solution. The sort of things that we like to
do is to analyze every RDS packet through deep packet
inspection and take appropriate actions. For example,
if message is targeted for DB services, identified
from RDS payload, then mangle the payload and/or
header as necessary and forward the message to
appropriate service(s). If message doesn't belong to
any services then re-inject, that is then process
through normal path in RDS. Which either send it up to
the user stack and/or route it to appropriate
destination node. If no action is needed then drop the
packet.

We have considered netfilter for RDS however it has a
major disadvantage that it only deals with sk_buff.
RDS module sits on top of TCP (rds_tcp) and IB
(rds_rdma), so messages arrive in form of skb (over
TCP) and scatterlist (over IB/RDMA). RDS messages over
TCP works with netfilter however messages in form of
scatterlist do not.

An alternative approach is to use eBPF for RDS packet
filtering. Using eBPF we can push RDS filters
dynamically from user-space to build firewalls. We
already have existing set of eBPF skb helpers in
kernel that we can use to process RDS messages in
struct sk_buff. Additionally, we like to add/extend
eBPF helpers to process messages that are in form
struct scatterlist. These eBPF helpers are also going
to be useful to other kernel modules that don't deal
with skb but scatterlist. Besides, there is a side
advantage of eBPF in RDS observability. For example,
today we don't have tool to dump full RDS packet.
There is tcpdump for rds_tcp however it is difficult
to parse tcpdump output since it doesn't preserve RDS
message boundaries.

With these set of goals, I am exploring adding eBPF
hooks into RDS and I would like to get feedback from
community.

sessions.title: Challenges migrating from NDIV to XDP
sessions.listing_title: Challenges migrating from NDIV to XDP
sessions.description:
We are currently studying the difficulty of porting of
our anti-DDoS solution PacketShield from NDIV to XDP.
Given that NDIV provides us exactly what we need to
achieve line-rate 10Gbps processing, we're extremely
careful not to lose too many aspects which have
participated to its current performance level. Thus
the presentation will start with a quick overview of
some key points that make NDIV perform well for our
use case, such as standardizing on the fastest NICs
and letting other ones implement missing features in
software, or how protocol elements are packed in
function arguments to reduce data manipulation along
the chain.

We already identified a number of shortcomings in XDP
that we're willing to discuss before trying to perform
possibly inappropriate changes. Some of them are
technical stuff that probably only require some work
or even maybe stealing code parts from NDIV, such as
passing L3/L4 checksums or packet classification
from/to the NIC. Some may require minor API updates,
such as passing outgoing network packets to the XDP
application so that the application can see both
directions and perform stateful filtering. Other
changes aim at making it easier for the application to
batch Rx processing, which we use to produce PCAP
network traces for troubleshooting.

Other limitations are probably much more philosophical
and will need some debates, such as the inability to
use loops in eBPF (we're looking up IP addresses and
VLANs from dynamic tables using a very fast and
efficient dichotomic approach), or exchanging data
with userland (we currently support on-the-fly
reconfiguration via /sys and we can sniff traffic at
line rate for debugging with no loss at 10G), making
us wonder if BPF is really suited to all use cases or
if we should allow an alternative way to register
native applications like NDIV currently supports.

Some preliminary information on NDIV :
  https://www.slideshare.net/ennael/kr2014-ndiv
  https://www.mail-archive.com/netdev@vger.kernel.org/msg129586.html
  https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/wtarreau/ndiv.git/

sessions.title: A PCC-Vivace Kernel Module for Congestion Control
sessions.listing_title: A PCC-Vivace Kernel Module for Congestion Control
sessions.description:
Many existing congestion control algorithms take a
harmful one-size-fits-all approach to congestion
control. First, they treat all traffic equally and try
to enforce fair sharing of bandwidth among competing
flows. However, different applications may have
different requirements for high quality service.
Streaming video can be sensitive to bandwidth
fluctuations, voice chat relies on low latency and
bulk downloads care only about flow completion time.
Second, congestion controllers need to deal with
highly dynamic and varied networks where hardwired
assumptions about the cause of packet loss or latency
inflation can be violated, leading to deficient
performance. Given such heterogeneity of application
goals and network conditions, applications stand to
benefit significantly from congestion control that
allows them to adopt different rate control
strategies.

In this work, we present a prototype kernel module
implementing the PCC-Vivace congestion control
algorithm [1].  Unlike many of the existing TCP
congestion control algorithms, which allow only
limited configuration, PCC-Vivace provides an explicit
utility function that allows developers to provide
weights to different performance metrics like
throughput, latency, packet loss and jitter.
PCC-Vivace then uses an online learning approach to
choose a connection bandwidth that maximizes utility.
This approach was recently shown to allow flexible
bandwidth sharing, a promising feature of congestion
control as increasingly diverse classes of
applications make use of the open Internet.
PCC-Vivace's online learning framework also allows it
to adapt to a variety of network conditions,
consistently delivering high performance.

Our talk discusses the challenges of implementing
PCC-Vivace in the Linux kernel and presents initial
results comparing the performance of this module with
other congestion controllers. We also demonstrate our
implementation's flexibility by creating and testing a
variety of utility functions.

References:
[1]  Mo Dong,   Tong Meng,  Doron Zarchy,
Engin Arslan, Yossi   Gilad, Philip Brighten Godfrey,
and Michael Schapira.
Vivace:  Online-Learning Congestion Control.
In NSDI, 2018.

different requirements for high quality service.
Streaming video can be sensitive to bandwidth
fluctuations, voice chat relies on low latency and
bulk downloads care only about flow completion time.
Second, congestion controllers need to deal with
highly dynamic and varied networks where hardwired
assumptions about the cause of packet loss or latency
inflation can be violated, leading to deficient
performance. Given such heterogeneity of application
goals and network conditions, applications stand to
benefit significantly from congestion control that
allows them to adopt different rate control
strategies.

In this work, we present a prototype kernel module
implementing the PCC-Vivace congestion control
algorithm [1].  Unlike many of the existing TCP
congestion control algorithms, which allow only
limited configuration, PCC-Vivace provides an explicit
utility function that allows developers to provide
weights to different performance metrics like
throughput, latency, packet loss and jitter.
PCC-Vivace then uses an online learning approach to
choose a connection bandwidth that maximizes utility.
This approach was recently shown to allow flexible
bandwidth sharing, a promising feature of congestion
control as increasingly diverse classes of
applications make use of the open Internet.
PCC-Vivace's online learning framework also allows it
to adapt to a variety of network conditions,
consistently delivering high performance.

Our talk discusses the challenges of implementing
PCC-Vivace in the Linux kernel and presents initial
results comparing the performance of this module with
other congestion controllers. We also demonstrate our
implementation's flexibility by creating and testing a
variety of utility functions.

[1]  Mo Dong,   Tong Meng,  Doron Zarchy,
Engin Arslan, Yossi   Gilad, Philip Brighten Godfrey,
and Michael Schapira.
Vivace:  Online-Learning Congestion Control.
In NSDI, 2018.

sessions.title: Suricata, an XDP adventure
sessions.listing_title: Suricata, an XDP adventure
sessions.description:
Suricata is an open source network intrusion detection
engine. It reconstructs the network traffic from level
2 all the way to the application layer by getting
individual packets from the capture device. The
upcoming 4.1 version will include eBPF and XDP
support. Suricata will be one of the pioneer software
systems to include these technologies.

The development did span over 2 years with some
preliminary works presented in previous Netdev events.
Suricata uses libbpf to interact with eBPF and XDP.
Multiple eBPF programs were created ranging from a
simple filter which was not possible with classic BPF
to a flow bypass technique implemented as eBPF socket
filter and in XDP. The CPU redirect is also
implemented to fix issues linked with asymmetrical
functions used in RSS load balancing.

Some problems and potential optimizations surfaced
during the development phase. For instance, the flow
bypass requires a flows table to be maintained by
Suricata. The per CPU structure is adequate for the
task but the flow table update from userspace appears
to be too costly as it requires a system call for each
element.  Another problem is the lack of an "official"
library for eBPF and XDP interaction. Libbpf is
supposed to go into that direction but had to be
improved to provide some basic services.

Tests results of eBPF and XDP integration show a
performance boost due to the bypass of an important
part of the flows and, as planned, eBPF socket filter
method has more CPU impact than the XDP one.

sessions.title: QUIC: Developing and Deploying a TCP Replacement for the Web
sessions.listing_title: QUIC: Developing and Deploying a TCP Replacement for the Web
sessions.description:
QUIC is an encrypted, multiplexed, and low-latency
transport protocol designed from the ground up to
improve transport performance for HTTPS traffic and to
enable rapid deployment and continued evolution of
transport mechanisms. QUIC has been globally deployed
at Google on thousands of servers and is used to serve
traffic to a range of clients including the Chrome
browser and the YouTube mobile video streaming app.
We estimate that 7% of Internet traffic is now QUIC.
QUIC is now maturing from a Google experiment to a
more complete Internet standard at the IETF.

This talk will provide an overview of the QUIC
protocol and the current state of its development and
deployment. We will describe motivations for
developing a new transport, QUIC's design and the
principles that guide it, and performance improvements
seen by various Google services due to QUIC. We will
also talk about performance bottlenecks in Linux UDP
seen at Google's servers, what we did to overcome
them, and what work remains to be done in the kernel
as QUIC becomes more widely deployed.

sessions.title: Building a Better NOS with Linux and switchdev
sessions.listing_title: Building a Better NOS with Linux and switchdev
sessions.description:
Whitebox switches, disaggregation, and open networking
are all the rage today. While the choice in white box
switches and "open" networking operating systems (NOS)
has proliferated in recent years, switching ASICs are
still predominantly programmed using SDKs and those
SDKs are primarily driven by userspace controllers.
The adherence to SDKs imposes a design constraint that
has a huge impact on the architecture of a NOS, its
choices for user APIs (how the switch is configured,
debugged and monitored) and the performance of the
control plane.

Over the past few years a lot of effort has been put
into a new approach for Linux - i.e., switchdev and
related in-kernel APIs. The result allows for a
simpler, cleaner NOS that fully leverages the Linux
kernel with the ASIC managed like any other hardware
in the system -- by a driver running in the kernel.
However, adoption of switchdev by ASIC vendors has
been lacking, with only one ASIC vendor at this point
writing a driver that works with switchdev.

This talk discusses typical software architectures for
network operating systems and introduces a path for
transitioning SDK based solutions to the switchdev
model.

sessions.title: LSDN - Manage complex (virtual) networks in cloud environment with Linux kernel facilities
sessions.listing_title: LSDN - Manage complex (virtual) networks in cloud environment with Linux kernel facilities
sessions.description:
We present a novel tool for effortless management of
complex (virtual) networks, especially those present
in todays cloud environment. The novelty comes from
the fact that we rely solely on the functionality
provided by the Linux kernel, mainly on the Traffic
Control (TC) subsystem with its recent features. To
our knowledge, this is the first tool of its kind
offering rich functionality without any external
modules such as Open vSwitch.

The core of our tool is a C library with a clean API
intended to be used with cloud orchestrators for
managing the whole network of a cloud. The API allows
you to create a model of the desired network. The
library then converts the model into set of TC rules,
mostly flower classifiers, which are loaded through a
netlink socket. This is a one-time action which does
not leave any running processes.  Also, the library
allows you to validate the network model prior to
loading it into the kernel, detecting common
configuration errors such as duplicated MAC addresses
of network nodes.

If support for machine migrations is required, our
simple daemon to keep the model in memory is used to
allow smooth reconfiguration. (In the future we want
to store needed metadata for migration in the kernel,
hence no daemon will be needed at all.)

Furthermore, we provide simple CLI tool which can read
networks from configuration files. The intended
use-case for this tool is for deployment without
orchestrators and it is also for automated testing of
the library.

The tool supports several back-ends (VLAN, VXLAN,
Geneve) for creating isolated virtual networks. In
these networks virtual ports can be configured via
simple API as well as stateless firewall (stateful
firewall is planned) and traffic shaping. The
corresponding part of virtual network on the
particular physical machine can be represented by
static or learning Linux kernel switch.

[1] https://github.com/asch/lsdn

sessions.title: Toward an eBPF-based clone of iptables
sessions.listing_title: Toward an eBPF-based clone of iptables
sessions.description:
Recently, there have been discussions in the Linux
networking community for the replacement of iptables
with an eBPF-based approach. So far, the submitted
work and ensuing discussions have been focused on the
performance impact of the equation - which favor the
eBPF approach. An approach to replace iptables with an
eBPF backend without disrupting the user control has
also been demonstrated [1].

This talk builds on the above context and proceeds by
presenting additional challenges that we feel need to
be addressed so as to obtain a fully-compatible clone
of iptables, i.e., to enable the eBPF-iptables tool to
accept traditional iptables commands, which are
emulated through the proper set of eBPF programs. Main
challenges here are:
(1) how to preserve the semantic of iptables rules,
given the different location of netfilter and eBPF
hook points;
(2) how to support (or at least cooperate) with
possible NATting rules;
(3) the selection of a matching algorithm that can
outperform current implementation (linear search), but
that is feasible by exploiting one of the eBPF maps
available in the kernel.
The new eBPF-iptables will allow users to benefit from
the performance improvement and not having to worry
about the operational impact of continuing to use the
iptables control interface.

[1]https://lwn.net/Articles/747551/

sessions.title: DIM - Generic Dynamic Interrupt Moderation library
sessions.listing_title: DIM - Generic Dynamic Interrupt Moderation library
sessions.description:
DIM lib is a net driver independent framework for
dynamically tuning interrupt moderation. DIM lib
exposes an API, which any net driver may use in order
to optimize its throughput, packet rate, latency and
interrupt rate.

This talk will describe details of DIM’s flow,
DIM’s algorithm, usage and performance benefits.

DIM lib was introduced upstream on kernel-4.16.
Drivers currently using it for dynamic interrupt
moderation include mlx5 (Mellanox), bcmsysport,
bcmgenet and bnxt (Broadcom).

sessions.title: How hard can it be? Adding Multipath TCP to the upstream kernel
sessions.listing_title: How hard can it be? Adding Multipath TCP to the upstream kernel
sessions.description:
A community project is underway to add Multipath TCP
to the upstream Linux kernel. This talk will briefly
introduce the audience to this TCP extension (RFC
6824) and mention some use cases already in
production.  The rest of the talk will be dedicated to
interactive discussions of the challenges in
converging on an upstream MPTCP implementation.

The current MPTCP implementation, already used by
millions of devices, cannot be proposed upstream as it
is due to its invasive architecture. This architecture
stems from the needs that were established when MPTCP
was still a research project.  However, now that the
protocol has stabilized and the implementation is
being used in production environments, the design
needs to be revamped for an upstream inclusion. But
this task is far from being easy as the MPTCP protocol
design tightly couples with TCP in order to look like
regular TCP on the wire, allowing it to traverse the
Internet with all its middleboxes and firewalls. This
makes the complexity of this upstream project a bit
unique in that additional protocols don't usually
overlap so much with an existing protocol - especially
a protocol as heavily used and optimized as TCP.

During this talk, we will present the different
challenges we have faced and we are still facing
today:



Protocol challenges, like a coupled receiver-window across the paths and a slightly changed dup-ACK behavior


Fitting within the existing TCP stack: performance, memory footprint, and maintenance should not be affected


Extending TCP capabilities in a generic way



For more information about this project:
https://github.com/multipath-tcp/mptcp_net-next/wiki

sessions.title: Smart Network Analytics with BPF using Skydive and CogNETive
sessions.listing_title: Smart Network Analytics with BPF using Skydive and CogNETive
sessions.description:
Efficient monitoring of large-scale networks poses a
delicate balance between capture granularity on the
one hand and the imposed overheads and performance
penalties on the other. Skydive is an open source
real-time network topology and protocol analyzer,
featuring smart network collection which is both
granular and efficient. Skydive allows for efficient
network monitoring@scale through Linux networking
features such as BPF and eBPF.  CogNETive is a
research operational analytics service that use
Skydive to create analytic insights.

In the talk we will present Skydive. Focus on the
usage of BPF in Skydive, and show how to capture
network information efficiently. We will share some
performance results showing the efficiency of Skydive
BPF capturing and will show how CogNETive uses that
data to produce useful analytic insights.

CogNETive uses several common open source components
(Grafana, ElasticSearch, Spark etc ...) to create a
layer of network analytics on top of Skydive.

sessions.title: Restructuring Endpoint Congestion Control
sessions.listing_title: Restructuring Endpoint Congestion Control
sessions.description:
This paper describes the implementation and evaluation
of a Congestion Control Plane (CCP), a new way to
structure congestion control at the sender by
refactoring the logic between the kernel and a
userspace program. With CCP, each
“datapath” that transmits and receives
packets, such as the Linux Kernel TCP, flexibly
summarizes information about the round-trip time,
packet receptions, losses, ECN, etc.  via a
well-defined interface.  Algorithms running atop CCP
use this information to control the datapath’s
congestion window or pacing rate.

We show that CCP enables, for the first time,
congestion control algorithms to be written once and
run on multiple datapaths. Experiments with our Linux
CCP implementation show that CCP algorithms behave
similarly to in-kernel algorithms, and incur modest
CPU overhead of a few percent. We also describe some
novel capabilities enabled by CCP’s refactoring
of congestion control functions, such as a congestion
manager for multiple flows and congestion control
using signal processing techniques, both running over
the Linux TCP stack.

sessions.title: Composing and configuring complex network interfaces exposed from network devices that contain a switch.
sessions.listing_title: Composing and configuring complex network interfaces exposed from network devices that contain a switch.
sessions.description:
With the addition of virtualization and the switch
control plane in the Linux kernel in the last few
years driven by the needs of the Cloud, the legacy
models and legacy data structures may not be providing
enough hooks for configuring and composing a network
interface.

With the switchdev model we are using netdevs both as
switch port representors and as the application's
network port in the VM/Container. Should the switch
port representors also provide hooks for composing the
network interface resources such as queues and MSIX
vectors? Will that scale well in future where network
interface in a VM or Container can be composed from
combination of pass-through and emulated queues and
MSIX vectors even crossing PCIe device boundaries.

Take the example of a multi-home network device; the
motivation is to spread a single switch port across
multiple PCIe devices so as to optimize
CPU-interconnect bandwidth in multi-socket systems. In
this situation, if the NIC-Switch is treating these
PCIE devices as one switch port and one network
interface, there will be a single netdev on top. If
one does not create separate netdevs per PCIe device,
how does one control the device resources, such as
queues per PCIe device? Does a 3-netdev model with

model might be being overextended to meet them and if
that is a good model.  The goal should be to come to a
consensus on how to address these going forward, so as
to avoid having multiple ways to do the same things in
the kernel. The paper will put forward a proposal that
will cater to various device composition needs as well
as device and switch configuration visibility needs,
for now and for future.

sessions.listing_title: UDP segmentation offload
sessions.description:
UDP segmentation was recently introduced to the Linux
kernel. Even though this is a new netdev features,
some existing devices (e.g. ixgbe, ConnectX-4, and
ConnectX-5) may be able to support it.

In this talk we will present our efforts towards
supporting UDP segmentation offload with existing
devices.  The limitations we've encountered. How we
overcome these limitations, and suggest potential
improvements to the Linux networking stack to
generalize our work and make driver development
easier.

sessions.title: IPsec/IKE tutorial/lab
sessions.listing_title: IPsec/IKE tutorial/lab
sessions.description:
The goal of the tutorial is to give the audience a
tour of the control and data-plane for IPsec in the
Linux kernel.  The tutorial will have two parts:
- one describing the kernel's datapath for IPsec, and,
- the second that goes over libreswan based tools that
  walk through the steps to set up the IKE (Internet
  Key Exchange) control-plane for that datapath

For the data-plane description, Sowmini will walk
through the basic network stack architecture for
traffic sent with IPsec. The goal will be to show the
"Life of a Packet" when IPsec is involved. We will
quickly go over the glossary/terminology around IPsec
and then walk through the stack internals to go over
the key data-structures and functions involved in the
datapath for IPsec.

This will be followed by a a quick rundown by Paul
Wouters on how the IKE control plane works and how to
configure IKE/IPsec using libreswan in some common
deployment scenarios such as remote access VPN,
hub-spoke networking and meshed cloud encryption.

Participants will be walked through the steps for
setting up IKE/IPsec on their Virtual Machines on
their laptop. A number of VMs will be made available
as targets to connect to using the different IKE
scenarios. These scenarios include some commonly
encountered roadblocks that will be used to teach
IPsec trouble-shooting issues. The lab session is
intended to be fully interactive, so we can go into as
much/little detail as time/interest permits.

sessions.title: Introduction to FRRouting
sessions.listing_title: Introduction to FRRouting
sessions.description:
The Free Range Routing(FRR) provides protocol daemons
for BGP, IS-IS, LDP, OSPF, PIM, and RIP. It is used by
many large ISPs, SaaS infrastructure data centres, and
Fortune 500 private clouds. More details at:
https://frrouting.org/

This instructor-led tutorial will cover basic
introduction to the FRRouting Suite and lead towards
advanced features on how FRR fits into the classic
Data Center.

The tutorial first half will be introduction to the
different components in FRR and how to get a basic
setup running.  We will then venture into basic setup
of OSPF/BGP/ISIS for a simple network.

In the second half we will discuss why and how OSPF
and BGP fit into the classic Data Center Architecture.
How RFC-5549 and Unnumbered interfaces changed
addressing and reachability in your network and how
this problem was solved in the Linux Kernel.  Finally
we will cover how EVPN solved L2 connectivity over L3
networks.  Users will be presented with working
examples and general knowledge of how to approach
using FRR for their routing needs.

sessions.listing_title: Workshop on IoT related MAC layers, header compression and routing protocols
sessions.description:
This workshop serves as a follow up and status update
on a similar workshop we have been running in an
earlier NetDev conference edition. It will continue on
topics discussed and bring new ones on the table.

In no particular order the agenda would roughly
cover:



ieee802154 and 6lowpan subsystem status update for the last kernel releases o Defining a userspace API to configure 6lowpan header compression options


Discuss what needs to be done for an ieee802154 hardMAC extension to the stack


Improve test coverage with hwsim, tdc, scapy & TITAN


Thoughts on software fallback implementations for ieee802154 CSMA and AACK


Thoughts on a LoRa subsystem (with SCHC addition to 6lowpan) for Linux



This workshop also aims to identify generic
requirements for the networking subsystem for IoT and
starting the process of addressing the gaps found. The
workshop will encompass related MAC layers, networking
protocols, adaptation layers, header compression,
routing protocols and application layers.

Note: We emphasize only on open protocols and
specifications as well as IPv6 instead of company
grown networking layers.

sessions.listing_title: Achieving super low latency for critical real world Internet applications
sessions.description:
This will be a discussion on the
possibilities and effort that is going to be required
to achieve super low latency (sub 10 msecs), high
throughput, secure, and highly reliable communications
for field applications and IoT. Applications include
real time safety (like traffic intersection
monitoring), remote surgery, industrial robotics,
sensitive control systems, etc. Emerging networking
technologies, such as 5G, are intended to provide the
transmission and network path latencies as low as 1
ms. In another dimension, machine learning is becoming
increasingly pervasive and will play a large role.

To facilitate discussion, we will (attempt :-) ) to do
a live physical demo of traffic intersection using a
slot car track. This will highlight the convergence of
machine learning, real time computation, and the need
for highly reliable, low latency communications in a
critical environments.

sessions.title: Evolving from AFAP: Teaching NICs about time
sessions.listing_title: Evolving from AFAP: Teaching NICs about time
sessions.description:
Network protocol designers of the 1970s all knew how
important it was to tailor each design to match the
speed & prop time of the links it was expected to
run over. Or rather, all designers except for a small
lunatic fringe who believed there was only one time
(As Long As It Takes) and only one speed (As Fast As
Possible). They called their protocol TCP/IP and the
Internet's success rests on their mania.

From the 80s through the early millennium, IP's AFAP
design let networks evolve painlessly as link
bandwidths doubled every year.  But the same physics
that limits processor clocks to around 2GHz makes
links >100Gbps a challenge. These limits mean we're
not only distributing computation over more CPUs
(which means more links since CPUs have to talk to
each other) but also adding additional links for
complex interconnect fabrics (since we can no longer
aggregate per-CPU traffic via a TOR with a 10x fatter
uplink).

'More links' rather than 'faster links' shifts the
network engineering focus from 'filling the link' to
'filling the network'. AFAP is great for filling
links. Unfortunately almost everything we know about
increasing network efficiency (e.g., minimize
head-of-line blocking by maximizing traffic entropy,
maximize total flow & minimize buffer pressure by
maximizing 'power') suggests that AFAP is a disaster
while AFAN -- As Fast as Necessary (but no faster) --
is close to optimal.

IP's AFAP model is embodied in our current NIC API --
we tell the NIC what to send but not when to send it.
I believe that our ability to build future high
efficiency networks depends critically on evolving the
NIC API to cover both 'what' & 'when'.  I'll try
to explain why and how, at least in Linux, the
evolution could be easy.
